title: Japji 28–33, whole
hook: the yogi's true ornaments and the ladder
tomorrow: a ladder needs a top. what are the five floors up there?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji 20 to 27: water for the hands, the Name for the mind, an ant that outweighs kings, and a house where everything sings.

Simran is rehearsing the send-off speech to the bathroom mirror in Maya's big gold hoops, because looking confident is half of it, right? Nanak met people who dressed the part too. The yogis of his day wore large earrings, carried a begging pouch, smeared ash on their skin. Pauri 28 doesn't mock any of it. It moves it inside: make contentment your earrings, modesty your pouch, meditation your ash, faith your staff. Then comes the strange part. A few pauris on, the Japji hands you a ladder, and right after that, says you have no power to climb.
screen: `HOOPS IN THE MIRROR.` → `CONTENTMENT FOR EARRINGS.` → `A LADDER, THEN NO POWER?`

segments.voice: Start with a word you've been saying for days. Each stanza of the Japji is a pauri, and in everyday Punjabi a pauri is a step, a stair. So the whole hymn is already built like a staircase. Pauri 28 adds a line worth carrying out of the room: make the whole human race your order. The yogis belonged to orders; Nanak's order is everyone. Pauri 29: let wisdom be your food, and compassion the one who serves it. Then pauri 32 says it outright. If my one tongue became a hundred thousand tongues, I would say the Name on every one, and these are the steps of the ladder; climb them, and you become one with the One. Now the puzzle. Pauri 33 opens: no power to speak, no power to be silent. No power to ask, or to give, or to live, or to die. The power is in that hand alone. So why the ladder? Here's a way to solve it. The steps aren't feats of strength. They're the Name, said and said again, the same small step a hundred thousand times. Pauri 33 just won't let you sign your name under the climb. You keep stepping. The holding isn't yours. Simran takes the hoops off, then puts them back on. She writes contentment on a sticky note and sticks it to the mirror.
screen: `A PAURI IS A STEP.` · `THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE, YOUR ORDER.` · `A HUNDRED THOUSAND TONGUES.` · `NO POWER TO SPEAK OR BE SILENT.` · then, large: `THE LADDER.`

segments.voice: Sit the way a yogi might, back straight, hands open on your knees, chin level. With each slow breath out, settle one of pauri 28's ornaments: contentment, then modesty, then faith, and start again. Let the posture hold you; you don't have to.
Japji 28: the start of pauris 28 to 33, where the yogi's ornaments move inside and the Japji hands you a ladder made of the Name.
For the road: the ladder, one small step of the Name at a time, held by a hand that isn't yours. Hoops on, sticky note up.

screen: `DAY 1766 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 6 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT ARE THE FIVE FLOORS AT THE TOP?`

howItsDone: Pauris 28 to 33 are recited as part of the Japji in the morning Nitnem; some Sikhs repeat Waheguru as simran, and teachers often point to pauri 32's ladder when they explain why the Name is said again and again.

fork.setup: a new club at school fills up with kids from one background, and someone says it should stay 'just our people.' what does pauri 28 suggest?
options: count the whole human race as your order, and keep the door open.
keep it close; an order is for people who already share your path.
skip clubs; real contentment means you never need a group at all.
fork.reveal: Nanak doesn't tell the yogis to stop belonging. he widens the order: make the whole human race your company.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a step or stair, and the name of each stanza of the Japji. the hymn is a staircase before pauri 32 even mentions a ladder.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pauri is just a verse number.
what it means: a pauri is a step, and pauri 32 calls the Name, said over and over, the steps of the ladder to the One.
what a scholar hears: the yogi's earrings, pouch, ash and staff from pauri 28 turned inward, and pauri 33's 'no power' setting the ladder in grace, not strength.

chat.says: maya lent me her big hoops so i LOOK confident at the send-off. is that fake??
options: wear them. pauri 28 just says the real earrings are inside: contentment.
kind of. pauri 28 says a Sikh shouldn't wear jewelry the way yogis did.
not fake. pauri 28 says the outside look shows what's inside, so go big.
chat.meaning: Pauri 28 doesn't mock the yogis' earrings; it moves the ornaments inside. Contentment is the pair that matters.

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib

pauri.meaning: a stanza of the Japji; in Punjabi, a step or stair

yogis.meaning: ascetics who wore earrings and ash and lived in orders

Nanak.meaning: Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, who wrote the Japji

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape puzzle (why hand someone a ladder and then say they have no power to climb?). Unity line: pauri 28's 'aaee panthee sagal jamaatee', paraphrased as 'make the whole human race your order'; confirm the paraphrase (some render it 'universal brotherhood your sect').

Pauri 28 ornaments: mundaa santokh (earrings), saram pat jholee (modesty the bowl/pouch), dhiaan kee bibhoot (meditation the ash), parteet the staff (danda). The voice lists earrings, pouch, ash, staff. Confirm.
Pauri 32: 'ik doo jeebhou lakh hohi...' the voice keeps 'a hundred thousand' (lakh, in the text) and leaves out the 'twenty times more'; 'pavrheeaa' as the steps of the ladder. Confirm.
'In everyday Punjabi a pauri is a step, a stair': standard meaning of ਪਉੜੀ/ਪੌੜੀ; the claim that the Japji is 'built like a staircase' is framed as a reading. Confirm.
Pauris 30–31 (the One who sees, unseen; storehouses in every world) are left out of the voice for length.
Gloss: ਜੋਗੀ for yogi (Punjabi form); confirm.
